Los Dodgers vuelven a reinar en el Oeste de la Nacional y buscan un tricampeonato pese a lesiones
CINCINNATI — Los Dodgers de Los Ángeles aseguraron su quinto título consecutivo de la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional y el 13ro en las últimas 14 temporadas al vencer el jueves 8-2 a los Rojos de Cincinnati.
“Es algo muy importante. Creo que mucha gente piensa que es solo un rito de paso (pero) no es fácil”, declaró el mánager de los Dodgers Dave Roberts. “Así que es algo de lo que todos estamos muy orgullosos, pero entendemos claramente que ese no es el objetivo final”.
Los Dodgers (93-60) disputarán los playoffs por 14 temporada consecutiva, con lo que igualan el récord que los Bravos de Atlanta establecieron de 1991-2005.
“Es el primer paso”, dijo Mookie Betts mientras se secaba el champán de los ojos. “Nos queda un largo camino por recorrer”.
La celebración en el terreno de juego fue algo calmada tras el último out el jueves. Pero los jugadores se soltaron en el vestuario, donde el champán y la cerveza salpicaron desde el suelo hasta el techo.
“Creo que es una de esas situaciones en las que, como en el béisbol se juega a diario, los jugadores se centran en rendir”, dijo Roberts. “Así que no hay muchos momentos para celebrar. Por eso es agradable ver a los chicos soltarse un poco”.
A pesar de todos sus laureles, los Dodgers creen que todavía tienen algo que demostrar.
El año pasado, el equipo pulverizó el récord de gasto de las Grandes Ligas con una nómina total de 515 millones de dólares, dando alas a críticas de que tienen una supuesta ventaja injusta.
“Lo que estamos creando aquí es especial”, afirmó Max Muncy. “Definitivamente no se le da el reconocimiento que merece. Todo el mundo se fija en la nómina, pero nunca hablamos de cómo hacemos las cosas bien, de cómo nos preparamos adecuadamente o de cómo cuidamos todos esos pequeños detalles. De eso no se habla”.
Los bicampeones defensores de la Serie Mundial aún pujan por el primer puesto de preclasificación de la Liga Nacional, que actualmente está en posesión de los Cerveceros de Milwaukee. Los Ángeles comenzó el día con una ventaja de tres juegos y medio sobre los Bravos (89-64) por el segundo puesto, pero está por detrás de los Cerveceros (95-57).
“Seguimos luchando por uno de los dos primeros puestos”, dijo Roberts. “Creo que hacemos bien celebrando, pero sin dejar que eso afecte a lo que sigue. Tenemos que tomar el vuelo y jugar contra los Gigantes mañana”.
Los Dodgers buscan convertirse en el primer equipo en conquistar tres campeonatos consecutivos de la Serie Mundial desde que los Yankees lo lograron de 1998 a 2000.
Este es el cuarto título divisional asegurado más temprano para los Dodgers. Aseguraron el Oeste de la Liga Nacional el 10 de septiembre de 2019, el 13 de septiembre de 2022 y el 16 de septiembre de 2023.
Los Ángeles aprovechará ese tiempo para recuperar lesionados. Eso empieza con Shohei Ohtani.
El cuatro veces Jugador Más Valioso ha estado en la lista de lesionados de 15 días desde el 8 de septiembre por una inflamación en el bíceps derecho y les dijo a los reporteros a principios de este mes que ya no lanzará más en lo que resta de temporada. La estrella de dos vías hizo swings desde un tee por primera vez el martes y se sintió bien. Se espera que regrese como bateador antes de que termine la temporada regular, aunque no está claro si podrá llegar al 100% de salud antes de octubre.
Roki Sasaki, en la lista de lesionados por una ampolla en el dedo medio, lanzó en una práctica de bateo en vivo el miércoles en Cincinnati y salió bien. Roberts indicó que su próxima aparición será como abridor.
Blake Snell salió prematuramente de la apertura del miércoles después de un inning por rigidez en la ingle izquierda. Su situación es incierta.
Se espera que el cerrador puertorriqueño Edwin Díaz, quien ha estado en la lista de lesionados desde agosto por una inflamación en el cuello, sea activado el viernes. El venezolano Edgardo Henríquez, un preparador de mesa en el bullpeb, está en la lista de lesionados por molestias en la parte baja de la espalda. Se le realizó una resonancia magnética en Los Ángeles el miércoles, que reveló una distensión lumbar, y su rehabilitación se pausará por unos días.
El primera base Freddie Freeman, aquejado por dolor en la rodilla derecha, regresó a la alineación el martes y cortó una mala racha de 3 hits en 30 turnos con tres imparables. Sumó otros dos hits el jueves.
Los Dodgers protagonizaron el mayor impacto de la fecha límite de cambios al adquirir a Tarik Skubal, ganador en dos ocasiones del premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, procedente de los Tigres. Skubal tiene marca de 3-2 con efectividad de 2.52 en ocho aperturas con los Dodgers.
La incorporación de Skubal convirtió a los Dodgers en los grandes favoritos en las apuestas para ganar la Serie Mundial. Pero después de comenzar la temporada con marca de 61-36, los Dodgers tienen registro de 31-24 desde la pausa del Juego de Estrellas.
Los Dodgers dejaron a 12 corredores en base y se fueron de 0 en 11 con corredores en posición de anotar en la derrota del miércoles ante los Reds, algo que, según Roberts, necesita mejorar.
“Se trata de poder rematar a los equipos cuando tenemos oportunidades. En la postemporada no se presentan muchas oportunidades. Hay que saber aprovecharlas”, dijo Roberts.

CINCINNATI — A few days off sounds pretty good right about now.
“I do think this team, as much as any team we’ve had, that week off is probably most beneficial,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said of locking down one of the top two seeds in the National League in order to get a first-round bye and five days off before starting the postseason.
Going into Thursday’s game, the Dodgers held a 3 ½-game lead over the Atlanta Braves for the second seed in the NL with a magic number of seven to clinch that first-round bye. The Dodgers trail the Milwaukee Brewers by three games for the top seed.
“It’s always helpful in the sense of giving your guys a break to reset,” Roberts said. “But given all the tax and where our guys are health-wise, to get that week would be huge.”
Blake Snell joined the long list of players with injury concerns when he left his start Wednesday after just one inning due to left groin tightness. The Dodgers also have questions about Shohei Ohtani (knee, biceps), Freddie Freeman (knee), Edgardo Henriquez (back), Andy Pages (hand), Roki Sasaki (blister) and Dalton Rushing (elbow).
Pages has been swinging a bat and hitting off the Trajekt machine this week, and it is “very likely” he will be activated from the IL during the homestand starting Friday, according to Roberts.
Ohtani has been “progressing” this week and is feeling “normal-ish” with no pain in his right arm or left knee, Roberts said.
“He’s doing everything he needs to do,” Roberts said. “I still don’t know when (his) time to return to play is. But everything that I hear is really positive.”
Snell could undergo an MRI to determine the severity of his groin injury. But he was optimistic after the game Wednesday that he had pulled back and left the game soon enough that it won’t be a serious issue and he might be able to make one more start before the end of the regular season.
“It’s all contingent on how he feels and potential imaging,” Roberts said. “It doesn’t make sense to just shut him down until the postseason if he can pitch. But again, if he’s not 100 percent to pitch, then we have no problem kicking the can.”
DIAZ RETURN
Right-hander Edwin Diaz completed his rehab assignment with Triple-A Oklahoma City on Wednesday and will join the Dodgers in Los Angeles this weekend with the expectation that he will be activated from the Injured List.
Diaz will be used in “low-leverage” situations, Roberts said, with a need to prove he can pitch well enough to assume a bigger role if he is on the postseason roster.
“I think, like anything, it should be a meritocracy,” Roberts said. “You have to earn the right of opportunities, but then you also have to perform, right? Eddie understands that. I think where we’re at now we just need guys to buy in, perform and go from there. That’s what he’s about.”
Roberts called Diaz’s final outing with OKC was “his best one yet.” Diaz pitched a scoreless inning, gave up a double and didn’t get a single swing-and-miss on any of 15 pitches.
“Quality of strike-throwing. Get guys out,” Roberts said of what he hopes to see from Diaz. “That’s probably it. As you get into the postseason, every inning’s leverage. So that’s kind of it. Quality of strike-throwing, and get guys out.”

CINCINNATI — The Los Angeles Dodgers have kept open the possibility that Shohei Ohtani will return before the end of the regular season, though they are up against a running clock.
Any progress is good progress for the Dodgers’ most important piece, so it was a good thing when Ohtani started up activity Tuesday and Thursday and didn’t report any discomfort in his bothersome biceps, balky left knee and tight neck.
“Feels normal…ish,” manager Dave Roberts said Thursday morning.
Advertisement
Ohtani went on the injured list late last week, ending a months-long injury saga and giving him a maximum of five additional regular season games to play in before another the playoffs. He is eligible to return as soon as Sept. 23, though Roberts did not commit to that timeline.
There are still steps for Ohtani to take. He swung off a tee on Tuesday, had Wednesday off from baseball activity and could hit off a coach’s pitching by the end of the week. He will need to face some sort of live pitching before he appears in a game and even then, the maximum of five games does not feel like a lot for him to get his timing right.
Especially since, given how the Dodgers tried kicking the can on shelving Ohtani, he will return after having taken just four plate appearances since Sept. 2. Ohtani, clearly compromised by his nagging injuries, had just six hits over his final 49 at-bats before hitting the IL.
They still need Ohtani, even if he is not 100 percent. The oldest lineup in baseball has shown its age. Even if Ohtani’s role on the postseason roster is simply to provide the threat of launching a ball into the seats, that is valuable in their quest for a third consecutive World Series title. The Dodgers’ first road trip without Ohtani since his arrival in 2024 has been noticeably different.
“It’s been a weird feeling because I talk to him all the time in the clubhouse,” Yoshinobu Yamamoto joked through interpreter Yoshihiro Sonoda. Yamamoto has instead had to rely on Roki Sasaki, “but he doesn’t really talk to me.”
Díaz’ place in the bullpen
Edwin Díaz will return to the Dodgers on Friday, but not as the club’s closer. Nothing is guaranteed for the guy the Dodgers gave $69 million to solve their ninth-inning problem and who now could be on the bubble for the postseason roster thanks to his 11.85 ERA.
Díaz, who has made only 16 major-league appearances thanks to arthroscopic elbow surgery and a later neck issue, has also pitched poorly in rehab. A five-run blowup on Sunday with Triple-A Oklahoma City caused the Dodgers to delay Díaz’s return. But a scoreless inning on Wednesday — albeit one in which Díaz gave up a 104 mph double and did not induce a single swing-and-miss — was enough for the Dodgers to bring him back to the big leagues.
“It was his best one yet,” Roberts said of Díaz, whose has a low bar to clear.
Advertisement
Díaz will return in lower-leverage situations and have to show prove over the final week of the regular season he deserves a spot in the Dodgers’ postseason bullpen, even if their list of right-handed relief options is thinning.
“I think like anything it should be a meritocracy,” Roberts said. “You have to earn the right of opportunities but then you also got to perform, right?”
Edgardo Henriquez was the club’s most trusted reliever before he went on the injured list on Monday. Subsequent imaging showed what Roberts dubbed a “low-grade” back strain, and the manager said he was “hopeful” that Henriquez could still be a postseason option.
Another potential solution, Sasaki, is now needed in the rotation after Blake Snell exited Wednesday’s start with left groin tightness. The Dodgers will know more about Snell’s fate once they return to Los Angeles and potentially get imaging done, but Sasaki is currently slated to pitch at some point next week against the San Diego Padres.
The Dodgers have also been cagey about Tyler Glasnow’s status. Roberts was vague after Glasnow’s last start, but said the right-hander “didn’t feel great” going into it. The Dodgers sent Glasnow directly to Los Angeles afterwards rather than have him travel with the club to Cincinnati, and Roberts said Glasnow’s preparation for Friday’s start has otherwise been normal.
Pages’ return imminent
Andy Pages will “very likely” return to the Dodgers’ lineup without playing in rehab games at some point during the six-game home stand that opens Friday. Pages has progressed quickly from left hand fracture and the Dodgers are banking on the All-Star’s defensive value in center field despite the chances he’ll struggle on offensive.
Pages moved from hitting softer baseballs to hitting normal ones this week and will hit off the Trajekt Arc machine to simulate live at-bats. There aren’t a lot of games to go around on a rehab assignment, anyway, though Oklahoma City did clinch a postseason berth on Wednesday (those games start next week).

The Los Angeles Dodgers are expected to activate Edwin Díaz from the injured list on Friday, but he will not slot back into closing games right away.
According to the Orange County Register's Bill Plunkett, Dave Roberts said the plan is to activate Díaz for the San Francisco Giants series, but to have him pitch in "low leverage" situations for the time being. Roberts also called the bullpen a "meritocracy" and said that Díaz needs to prove himself.
Díaz was the National League Reliever of the Year last year and has won three career Reliever of the Year Awards. The Dodgers gave him a three-year, $69 million deal in the offseason, but he has had a terrible season.
Through his first six games, he had a 10.50 ERA and blew a save. He then underwent a procedure to remove loose bodies from his elbow. After returning, he posted a 12.91 ERA in nine games, blowing three saves. The Dodgers placed him on the injured list with neck inflammation on Aug. 18 and are hoping for the best version of him this time.
Díaz has noted that he thinks fixing his arm angle will help him, but it's a results-based business. He will have to prove he can pitch like the Dodgers expected him to be, and the Dodgers need him more now than ever.
Since the All-Star Break, the Dodgers bullpen has a 4.34 ERA, ranked 20th in baseball. The bullpen also has a 10.4% walk rate, the seventh-worst in baseball. Dodgers relievers have also given up 24 home runs in the second half. If Díaz can come back and pitch like an All-Star, it will go a long way in fixing the bullpen woes. The team is currently without Edgardo Henriquez, so they need a reliable right-hander in the bullpen.
Roberts also confirmed that outfielder Andy Pages (hand) is expected to rejoin LA during upcoming homestand without requiring a minor-league rehab assignment.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are on the verge of clinching the National League West for a 13th time in the past 14 seasons, but it’s coming with notable questions, if not concern, regarding health heading into October.
Shohei Ohtani, Dalton Rushing, Andy Pages and Edgardo Henriquez are among the team’s key contributors who currently are on the injured list. Blake Snell could find himself there after leaving his start on Wednesday due to left groin tightness.
Henriquez was the most recent addition to the IL, due to an official diagnosis of low back discomfort. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts suggested there was the potential for an oblique issue as well.
Edgardo Henriquez MRI results
Henriquez returned to Los Angeles before the end of the road trip in order to meet with doctors and undergo testing. According to Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic, an MRI revealed Henriquez suffered a back strain.
Edgardo Henriquez has a “low-grade” back strain, Dave Roberts said. Dodgers are “hopeful” to have him back for the postseason.
— Fabian Ardaya (@FabianArdaya) September 16, 2026
Prior to having the MRI results, Roberts had previously expressed a hope Henriquez would return in time for the postseason. That possibility will hinge on his recovery process.
What is already guaranteed is the hard-throwing righty won’t pitch again during the 2026 regular season because of being ineligible to get activated within the remaining timeframe. Henriquez’s status is further reason for the Dodgers to secure one of the top two seeds in the NL and thus a first-round bye in the postseason.
Doing so would push the Dodgers’ first playoff game to Oct. 3 with the start of the NL Division Series.
Henriquez allowed two runs last Sunday against the Miami Marlins in what was his final appearance before going on the IL. He retired just two batters after entering in the eighth inning, trying to protect a 3-0 lead.
Henriquez gave up two singles and a walk, which loaded the bases. Then another base hit drove in two runs, prompting Dodgers manager Dave Roberts to turn to Tanner Scott.
The 24-year-old finishes his 2026 season with 61 appearances in what became a true breakout year. Henriquez went 4-1 with a 2.85 ERA and also set a Dodgers record for the fastest pitch thrown on a strikeout earlier this year.
Henriquez was an option to receive more save opportunities moving forward as he continued to impress in high-leverage situations while others in the bullpen struggled. That could still hold true, but now health becomes paramount.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are on track to win the NL West and probably earn a first-round bye in the postseason. That comes despite a recent onslaught of injuries. Los Angeles is not unaccustomed to a stacked injury list, but the Dodgers' elite depth — aided by a top-ranked farm system and unrivalred spending power — makes them uniquely resilient.
What has helped L.A. win back-to-back World Series titles, however, is their knack for getting healthy at the right time and charging into October at full strength. The Dodgers are hoping to do just that, again. Let's rank six potential returners who could make an outsized impact.
6. RHP Edwin Díaz
Should Edwin Díaz actually come back for the playoffs? He got rocked in his recent Triple-A rehab appearance. The Dodgers' prized $69 million investment has only pitched 13.2 innings in the majors this season, with a disastrous 11.85 ERA (not a typo). Díaz has not looked right at any point.
While the Dodgers presumably want such an expensive and accomplished reliever on the postseason roster, it may be smarter to punt on this season entirely. Díaz is more than capable of rebuilding confidence and getting healthy in the offseason, but it's unclear if L.A. can rely on him in even the lowest-leverage spots currently. Rather than playing with fire, so to speak, the Dodgers should probably lean on their spectacular bullpen depth and keep Díaz on the sidelines. The risk far outweighs the potential reward of rushing him back.
That said, when healthy, Díaz has a long track record as one of MLB's best closers. We know he can electify in the late innings. If the Dodgers are confident for reasons we on the outside aren't privy too, never say never on a triumphant turnaround.
5. RHP Roki Sasaki
Through two seasons, the Rōki Sasaki experience has not quite lived up to expectations for Dodgers fans. Hailed as the best Japanese pitching prospect in a generation, the 24-year-old looks an awful lot like... a prospect. A work in progress. Los Angeles expected immediate results. Now, the Dodgers are hoping Sasaki can iron out command issues against MLB competition. He appeared briefly in the minors this season, but the Dodgers are effectively all-in on Sasaki as a major league pitcher.
Sasaki is expected to recover from a blister before the playoffs, although the Dodgers are uncertain about his exact role. The rotation is much too deep for Sasaki to start in a must-win environment. He was effectively L.A.'s closer last October — a role in which he thrived — but a healthy Tanner Scott removes Sasaki from consideration for that role. Expect him in the bullpen, probably handling bulk work if one of L.A.'s starters is forced out early.
4. C Dalton Rushing
Dalton Rushing was recently returned to the IL after suffering a setback in his recovery from UCL surgery. He's done catching for the season, but L.A. still hopes the 25-year-old can return as a hitter. Of course, if Rushing is effectively relegated to DH, it will be hard to get him in the lineup with Shohei Ohtani also on the roster. Rushing could end up as a situational, pinch-hitter type in October, if he's even on the roster.
It's a credit to how deep the Dodgers are that Rushing being "situational," rather than essential, is even in the cards. The rookie backstop cooled off after the All-Star break, but he's still phenomenally talented. He has a .798 OPS and 120 wRC+ as a rookie, with 12 home runs in only 250 at-bats.
Rushing is stuck behind Will Smith on the org chart, which complicates his future somewhat, but the Dodgers will find ways to use him if he's available.
3. RHP Edgardo Henriquez
The Dodgers hope Edgardo Henriquez can return from a low-grade back strain come the playoffs. The 24-year-old fireballer has quickly established himself as one of baseball's most dominant relievers. He has a 2.85 ERA and 1.03 WHIP with 71 strikeouts in 60.0 innings pitched this season; he ranks in MLB's 99th percentile for both hard-hit rate (27.1 percent) and average fastball velo (100.8 mph).
Henriquez is more than a hard-thrower. He misses barrels and limits explosive hits, able to force groundballs or lifeless bloopers just as often as he forces swing-and-miss. He leans heavily on his four-seam and sinker combo, with a sweeping slider that leaves opposing hitters gasping for air (.191 xwOBA). Should Henriquez return in time, the Dodgers can plug him right into high-leverage spots and expect results. He's the real deal, folks.
2. OF Andy Pages
Andy Pages is back in the batting cage after breaking his hand in mid-August. The Dodgers' centerfielder has enjoyed a proper breakout campaign, posting a .797 OPS and 119 wRC+ with elite defensive metrics and 12 stolen bases. In terms of fWAR, or wins above replacement, Pages ranks third among L.A. positional players (3.9), behind only Shohei Ohtani (6.8) and Max Muncy (4.0).
The Dodgers really need Pages on cleanup duty in centerfield. He covers so much ground and features a killer arm, which wipes runs off the board. Pages' bat cooled down before the injury, but he's still far more dangerous than L.A.'s alternatives — although the recent promotion of top prospect Josue De Paula does create a difficult decision for manager Dave Roberts, assuming the DH spot reverts back to Ohtani.
Speaking of which...
1. DH Shohei Ohtani
This was obvious, yeah? Shohei Ohtani is currently on ice as he attempts to shed bicep and knee problems. That said, the Dodgers plan to get him back before the regular season ends — and it would be absolutely shocking if Ohtani weren't leading off in Game 1 of the Dodgers' first postseason series.
The nagging nature of Ohtani's injuries mean he won't take the mound again in 2026, but he's still the most valuable hitter in the majors, on balance. Yes, Yordan Álvarez and Pete Crow-Armstrong are enjoying better seasons, but Ohtani is the man you want at the plate in a big spot. Drafting a fantasy team, he's your No. 1 pick. So on and so forth.
After spending the early portion of his MLB career on an unserious Angels team, Ohtani is two-for-two in the World Series since joining the Dodgers. He has consistently come up large in the playoffs. Assuming Ohtani is anywhere close to 100 percent, the Dodgers are once again (easy) favorites to win it all.

Dodgers news: Dave Roberts' plan for bullpen game vs. Reds after Blake Snell injury appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Los Angeles Dodgers will turn to Justin Wrobleski and Landon Knack for the bulk of Thursday's series finale vs. the Cincinnati Reds after Blake Snell's early exit Wednesday night.
Wrobleski will start at Great American Ball Park, while Knack will return to the active roster and follow him as Los Angeles navigates its pitching depth. The Dodgers will option Bobby Miller to Triple-A Oklahoma City in the corresponding move after he worked 2 1/3 innings Wednesday.
The Athletic's Fabian Ardaya took to X, formerly Twitter, relaying manager Dave Roberts' pitching plan as the Dodgers adjust following Snell's unexpected departure with left groin tightness.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"Justin Wrobleski will start and he and Landon Knack will take the bulk of the game tomorrow. Bobby Miller is being optioned for Knack, Dave Roberts said."
Snell felt his groin "grab" during his pregame bullpen Wednesday but still made his scheduled start. The two-time Cy Young winner threw one scoreless inning on 19 pitches before the Dodgers removed him as a precaution.
His departure forced the Dodgers to use six relievers over the final seven innings in their 6-2 loss. Miller accounted for 2 1/3 of those frames after the club recalled him Monday when Edgardo Henriquez went on the injured list.
Wrobleski, meanwhile, has pitched out of the bullpen since returning from a left forearm injury on September 1. The 2026 MLB All-Star was already on the active roster, while Knack was with the Reds as organizational pitching depth ahead of his recall.
Los Angeles is 92-60 after Wednesday's loss. The San Diego Padres' 9-3 win over the Colorado Rockies kept the Dodgers from clinching the NL West that night and left the magic number at one. A victory Thursday against the Reds, or a Padres loss, would give the Dodgers their fifth consecutive division crown.

CINCINNATI — Now what?
Roki Sasaki threw 48 pitches in four simulated innings to Dodgers hitters on Wednesday afternoon, testing the blister on his right hand that landed him on the injured list. He gave up a home run to Eliezer Alfonzo but otherwise “was good,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said.
Sasaki threw with Dermabond on his injured finger. A surgical adhesive used to close cuts and incisions, pitchers are allowed to use it in games if their team gets permission from MLB in advance.
“He came out of it well,” Roberts said. “So we have to huddle up here and figure out what’s his role. What does it look like as we sit here on the 17th or 18th of September, whatever? So the number one most important thing is that he came out of that session well, and then now we got to figure out how to plug him in. He’s going to be important, but I just don’t know right now what role.”
Sasaki seemed destined for a bullpen role again this postseason, a role he assumed successfully last year. But the Dodgers have reason to hesitate on turning Sasaki into a reliever with Blake Snell leaving his start after just one inning on Wednesday night and Tyler Glasnow’s status.
Glasnow flew back to Los Angeles after his start in Miami. It was the second consecutive start in which Glasnow was not sharp and this time he could be seen in the dugout stretching out his back. But after the game, he said his back felt fine and Roberts said Glasnow threw a “normal” bullpen session in L.A. on Wednesday and is scheduled to make his next start on Friday night.
Sasaki is penciled in now to start during the series against the San Diego Padres in Los Angeles next week and remain a starter at least for now.
“One can argue it’s best to take down a couple starts, keep him built up, because if something does happen, he’s built up,” Roberts said. “The other side is you can assimilate him into the ’pen and get comfortable in that role – if that is the role.
“But again, I don’t want to speak out of turn and say that’s done, because it’s not.”
NO SHO
The Dodgers are about to complete their first road trip in three seasons without Shohei Ohtani. Yoshinobu Yamamoto might have missed Ohtani more than any other of his teammates.
“It’s been a weird feeling because I talk to him all the time in the clubhouse,” Yamamoto joked through his interpreter when asked about Ohtani’s absence. “All I have is Roki, but he doesn’t really talk to me.”
Back in Los Angeles, Ohtani has been receiving treatment for his knee and bicep injuries. According to Roberts, Ohtani began swinging a bat, hitting off a tee this week.
“There’s going to be a consistent build-up,” Roberts said. “Don’t know when the time of return to play is, but today was positive, and hopefully we can just keep building towards that.”
Ohtani will be eligible to be activated from the IL next Wednesday. Whether he is ready to play that day or shortly after, Roberts said the expectation is that Ohtani will return in time to play before the regular season ends on Sept. 27.
“I do,” Roberts said. “Whether it happens or not is to be determined. But I do expect him to be back to play in some regular-season games. Don’t know how many of them.”
COMING/GOING
Right-hander Edwin Diaz made his fifth rehab appearance with Triple-A Oklahoma City on Wednesday, pitching a scoreless inning to close out the Comets’ playoff berth-clinching victory. Diaz did allow a double to a fellow big-leaguer on rehab, Miguel Andujar.
Meanwhile, Edgardo Henriquez returned to Los Angeles and underwent an MRI, which confirmed the diagnosis of a “low-grade back strain,” Roberts said. He won’t be eligible to pitch again in the regular season but Roberts said the Dodgers are “hopeful” he could come back for the postseason.
Left-hander Kris Bubic was activated from the 60-day IL before Wednesday’s game and right-hander Paul Gervase was returned to OKC. In order to clear a spot on the 40-man roster for Bubic, Triple-A outfielder Ryan Ward was designated for assignment.
Right-hander Landon Knack will be added to the active roster before Thursday’s game and Bobby Miller will be returned to OKC.
ALSO
Outfield prospect Charles Davalan (the 41st pick in last year’s draft) was named MVP of the Class-A Midwest League and Great Lakes manager Jair Fernandez was named the league’s Manager of the Year. Davalan hit .292 with 24 home runs and a .937 OPS. He is scheduled to play in the Arizona Fall League, where he is expected to start testing out a possible conversion to second base.
UP NEXT
Dodgers (LHP Justin Wrobleski, 11-5, 3.78 ERA) at Reds (RHP Brady Singer, 6-14, 5.38 ERA), Thursday, 9:40 a.m., SportsNet LA, 570 AM

item.content:encoded:
Edgardo Henriquez’s regular season was already effectively over once the Dodgers placed the hard-throwing pitcher on the 15-day injured list Monday with low back discomfort.
Henriquez, whose 103.6-mph fastball was the fastest pitch thrown by a Dodger since at least 2008, was diagnoesed with a low back strain. Bill Plunkett of the Southern California News Group reported Wednesday, Sept. 16, that the pitcher is “hopeful” he can return in October after getting the results of an MRI exam.
“Hopeful” and “probable” can be a world apart. In Henriquez’s case, it’s unclear whether his hope stems from the severity of his diagnosis, or from his faith that the Dodgers will play deep enough into the postseason to give him a chance to recover.
In either event, the Dodgers’ bullpen without Henriquez is a very different one than what they hoped to carry in their quest to three-peat as World Series champions.
Henriquez’s fastball touched 103.6 on June 2 in a game against the Arizona Diamondbacks, and again on Aug. 29 in a game against the Detroit Tigers.
Speed is just one facet of Henriquez’s game. His 71-to-25 strikeout-to-walk ratio, combined with only 37 hits allowed in 60 innings, gave the right-hander an at-times untouchable arsenal.
No right-handed pitcher had made more appearances for the Dodgers this season than Henriquez’s 61. Without him, manager Dave Roberts might have to get creative.
Right-hander Roki Sasaki, a starter during the regular season and a reliever during the team’s 2025 World Series run, might return in a relief role once he’s recovered from a finger blister. Edwin Diaz, who is currently on a rehab assignment of his own, struggled mightily in the closer’s role this season — but might be needed in some capacity just to get the Dodgers through to the end of the postseason.
Diaz, a three-time All-Star, had an 11.85 ERA in 16 appearances with the Dodgers before landing on the injured list with a neck injury Aug. 16.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers key reliever Edgardo Henriquez got the official diagnosis for his lower-body injury that has him on the injured list.
Henriquez has a "low-grade" back strain, and the team is "hopeful" he'll be back for the postseason, manager Dave Roberts said.
Roberts described the MRI results as "positive," which should be a relief for fans hoping to get their best bullpen arm back in time for the playoffs.
The Dodgers placed him on the 15-day injured list, meaning that he is not eligible to return until September 29th, effectively ending his regular season.
All eyes will be on Henriquez as we look toward October, when he is expected to be a high-leverage arm, possibly even the closer if he is able to get back to pitching again soon.
Why Henriquez is so important for the Dodgers
Henriquez has a 2.62 ERA, with a 2.50 FIP. He misses the barrel of the bat, strikes out hitters, and limits home runs like one of the best relievers.
He throws triple digits, which may explain his back issue, but the pitch's movement and growing command make it a deadly weapon out of the bullpen.
While he lacks the high-leverage experience of players like Edwin Diaz and Tanner Scott, Henriquez carries himself confidently and exudes a strong presence whenever he takes the mound.
It is unclear how quickly the Dodgers will pull the trigger on Henriquez in the playoffs for a high-leverage role, but given what he has proven this year, they will try to lean on him as much as his health permits.

The Los Angeles Dodgers will be without relief pitcher Edgardo Henriquez for the remainder of the regular season. The 24-year-old was placed on the 15-day injured list on Sept. 14.
Henriquez’s injury was initially labeled as lower back discomfort. With further imaging and testing, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said the injury is a “low-grade back strain,” per MLB.com’s Sonja Chen.
Although Edgardo Henriquez’s regular season is over, he still remains someone that Los Angeles can get back for the postseason. Dave Roberts said that he remains “hopeful” that Henriquez can return in October.
Edgardo Henriquez’s Dominant 2026 Season
Coming off limited MLB experience, Edgardo Henriquez displayed the best pitching of his career in 2026. The high-velocity right-handed pitcher was a reliable piece of the Dodgers’ bullpen throughout the season.
In 61 appearances, Henriquez finished with a 4-1 record, 2.85 ERA, and 1.03 WHIP across 60.0 innings pitched. He also added 11 holds and two saves in the season.
Henriquez was among the hardest-throwing pitchers in the league. The 24-year-old’s fastball reached as fast as 104 miles per hour this season.
“He hit 103 mph or higher 17 times, more than any Major League pitcher not named Jacob Misiorowski (140 pitches) or Mason Miller (33 pitches). But Henriquez became more than just a hard thrower this year, developing the command and the confidence to be a leverage weapon for the Dodgers,” MLB.com’s Sonja Chen wrote.
Dodgers Still Searching For Answers on Edwin Diaz’s Status
The Los Angeles Dodgers made closer Edwin Diaz the most expensive reliever in MLB last offseason, signing him to a three-year, $69 million contract.
Diaz’s first season with the Dodgers has not been what many expected. While dealing with injuries, Diaz’s season stats include a 2-2 record, 11.85 ERA, and 2.56 WHIP across 13.2 innings pitched.
While dealing with inflammation in his neck, Edwin Diaz has remained on the injured list since Aug. 18. He has since begun a rehab assignment, with results that haven’t gone well.
The 32-year-old allowed five runs in a rehab appearance in Triple-A Oklahoma City on Sept. 13. Dave Roberts says that if Diaz’s game doesn’t improve, he could be left off the Dodgers’ postseason roster, according to The Athletic’s Fabian Ardaya.
“He needs to pitch better,” Roberts also mentioned. “I think the world of him. The baseball card looks great. But it’s like, where we’re at, there’s got to be something for us to be able to hang our hat on. And he knows that.”
Diaz made another rehab appearance on Wednesday, pitching one scoreless inning. However, he didn’t produce a swing-and-miss and gave up a double, says Ardaya.

item.content:encoded:
gambit – noun
a chess opening in which a player risks one or more pawns or a minor piece to gain an advantage in position
Now, if your mind immediately went to the Marvel Comics character and you were confused, fair enough. Here's the clip you likely thought of, so we can all feel better and get to the heart of the essay.
And for the record, Freddie Freeman is hardly a minor piece, but giving up a major piece for tactical advantage is called a sacrifice, which wouldn't be appropriate given the circumstances here, as Freeman returned to the lineup for the September 15 game against the Cincinnati Reds.
A funny thought occurred to me while watching Freddie Freeman these last few months:
"Where did his power go? He sure seems like he's hitting into more double plays than I remember."
Looking at Freeman's stats for the year, apart from the power and RBI numbers being down a bit, nothing looks amiss. Honestly, I originally dismissed the feeling that something was wrong because Freeman was hitting up a storm for about a month after the All-Star Break.
There wasn't much power behind it, but when someone has a slash line of .367/.402/.411 over 24 games starting from the All-Star Break, pointing out fault feels like searching for a fly in the ointment. Yes, Freeman only had four doubles, eight RBIs, and nearly three times as many strikeouts as walks, but the overall body of work looked pretty good.
Freeman had a solid couple of games in Denver where he hit for doubles power and used the entire field. However, since the Denver series, where Freeman was hitting for average, he's just not.
When you aren't hitting for either average or power, alarm bells tend to finally ring.
Power drained
On September 9, Freeman was kept out of the lineup for right knee soreness and was considered day-to-day. To his credit, Dave Roberts did mention Freeman's slump on September 9.
Roberts said there was no one incident that caused Freeman's knee soreness, but he believes it has impacted his performance at the plate lately.
"Freddie does a really good job of hitting against his front side, and then when you can't do that with your front side, your right knee, then you're compromised," Roberts said. "I see there's a lot more swing-and-miss the last few days. That's just not who he is."
In the 18 games since the Colorado series until the start of play on September 15, Freeman has a slash line of .215/.338/.292. He does have his only home run of the second half, and his strikeouts-to-walk ratio is about 1.5/1 instead of 3/1 earlier in the year.
The problem is more of the eye test: Freeman is starting to finally look, and maybe move, like his age.
The splits on Baseball Savant from last year to now tell a pretty glaring tale: if you want to beat Freeman in 2026, go low and in. Also, Freeman feasted on center-cut pitches last year, not so this year.
I'm not a hitting expert, but having a diminished knee would make it harder to rotate to hit stuff middle in. On the September 13 broadcast of the finale against the Miami Marlins, Dontrelle Willis pointed out how Freeman is compromised rotationally generally, as pitches he would normally drive the other way are being weakly hit.
Even after Freeman hit a career-high and now league-high in double plays on Sunday, the Dodgers are not seriously entertaining putting Freeman on the injured list, per Katie Woo of The Athletic:
"I think it's one of those things where we've got to manage it … just pick spots to give him an off day here or there," Roberts said. "Again, we've just got to make sure he's at optimal health when we finish the season. So I think that he might not love it, but giving him a day off here or there might be beneficial."
The Dodgers don't believe an IL stint is necessary. Instead, Roberts is working in frequent off days. That's rare for Freeman, who hasn't played in fewer than 147 games in any season as a Dodger. Freeman had a scheduled day off over the Dodgers' previous nine-game homestand and also served as the designated hitter twice in that span. He wasn't in the lineup in the last game of the homestand on Wednesday, and following a team travel day, he also sat out Friday's game.
[Emphasis added.]
Freeman insists he feels fine.
Freeman hitting into two double plays and having a key miscue that contributed to the season and series loss to the Miami Marlins seems to indicate otherwise. It's worth noting that Freeman hit another tailor-made ground ball to second on a pitcher's pitch in his final at-bat that likely would have turned into another double play had Mookie Betts not doubled earlier in the frame.
"Just talking to him today, he said he felt good," Roberts said. "Obviously, the swings don't indicate that, don't validate that. On the defense, he's obviously not moving as well as he's used to.
"I think that he's doing anything and everything he can to prepare. But yeah, the last week, it's pretty obvious that he's not himself in the box."
Freeman won't be in Monday's starting lineup, Roberts said, but should play Tuesday…
[Emphasis added.]
Much like the sense one had when watching the Americanized remake of the original 1954 classic Gojira, Godzilla: King of the Monsters, one would expect a sense of deja vu right now, even with character actor Raymond Burr long dead.
Japanese Original, American Remake
I am typically not one to mince words, and I shall not do so here. Along with Dustin Nosler of Dodgers Digest, I was dead on the money regarding the Dodgers' malpractice in not acting decisively on Ohtani and his reluctance to admit injury in the face of personal dogma of success.
I argued that the Dodgers had bungled spectacularly, and events worked themselves out to prove my initial hypothesis correct on all fronts. Now the team has backed itself into a corner regarding Ohtani.
Contrary to what some might think, I did not enjoy being right. Frankly, I am correct often enough that I do not need the constant validation, unless it comes from either the Dodgers broadcast team or national media. (In which case, gimme.)
On September 11, Katie Woo of The Athletic wrote an op-ed recently that pulled few punches:
Nobody is blameless in the Shohei Ohtani injury saga. Not the Los Angeles Dodgers' front office, which should have been more proactive in protecting the team's biggest star. Not Ohtani, who downplayed the severity of his symptoms. And while hindsight is always 20-20, there were warning signs throughout the last few weeks that suggested a stint on the injured list was the safest course of action if the organization wanted to give its prized star the best possible chance at healing in time to begin the Dodgers' quest to win three straight World Series.
As the Dodgers prepare to be without Ohtani until Sept. 23 at the earliest, their biggest concern has become a reality. When Ohtani — who is expected to be placed on the injured list on Friday — does return, there is no guarantee he'll be in optimal condition for the postseason.
[Emphasis added.]
Um, excuse me? To quote one of the finest bits of media from the 2010s, I get to channel Chris Taylor for once and declare the following:
I know, Ms. Woo means nobody relevant, but words matter, and any excuse for referential comedy is a good one.
"I think that if it were a postseason game tomorrow, (Ohtani) would be in the lineup," manager Dave Roberts said Wednesday afternoon, hours before announcing Ohtani would be placed on the IL. "I think that now you're talking about two weeks, 14 days. I feel that that's substantial. He'll be in a much better place than he was today. Is it going to be to 100 percent? Probably not. But I do think that with this time that we're taking now he'll be in an adequate spot to finish the season."
Adequate is a far cry from healthy. It is fair to question how Ohtani was handled in the second half. Should he have attempted a pitching comeback, knowing his physical health was limited? Should the Dodgers have stopped that push sooner, or placed him on the injured list earlier? In their first season of managing Ohtani as a full-season two-way player, there was always going to be some trial and error. That was acknowledged from the start of the season by both Roberts and president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman. And in fairness, there was a cognizant effort to keep Ohtani as rested as possible, including a season-long six-man rotation and an attempt to maneuver Ohtani's starts to line up on games prior to a team off day, when possible.
Hindsight is generally 20/20. I am sure if the Dodgers were armed with foreknowledge in a do-over, they would not have Ohtani's best pitching starts of the year be in Houston and San Francisco … in May.
At the risk of retreading previously covered ground, we shall conclude this portion with Roberts' regret, especially considering that Ohtani tweaked his arm in his last played game and did not immediately tell anyone about it:
Looking back, it is something Roberts wish happened a week ago.
"I think if we look right now, here today, I would love to go back and put him on the IL," the manager said. "But I did feel at that moment in time, we all felt that giving him four days was sufficient. He was agreeable. Getting him out there on Monday with the hope that he would be able to play tonight. But where we're at right now, sure."
The Dodgers should have followed their own advice or learned from their handling of Ohtani to send Freeman back to Los Angeles for ten days before arriving in Cincinnati.
They didn't.
The Dodgers have calculated that whatever value Freeman can generate in the waning days of the season is greater than the potential benefit of having Freeman recuperate for ten days, having three days against the already-eliminated San Francisco Giants to use as a tune-up. Hence, the title of this essay: the Freeman Gambit.
Yesterday's game showed promise, even with a couple of moments that made one grimace. Freeman talked about how his three-hit performance likely ensured he would play on September 16.
Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic reported Roberts' comments on the health issues of players like Ohtani, Freeman, and Edgardo Henriquez after the Dodgers clinched their fourteenth consecutive postseason appearance:
"I think right now it's front of mind, it's not great," Roberts said. "But I will say this: Once you get to October, athletes have a magical way of feeling better. It happens every single year, where there's that extra adrenaline that athletes get when you get to the postseason."
The Dodgers still boast what is likely baseball's most talented roster and an established track record of postseason success that might be enough to make history. That was the heart of Roberts' toast: that the Dodgers have not yet played their best baseball.
They still can.
"We just haven't really gotten everyone all synced up at the same time," Muncy said. "So it is a scary thought to think what we could possibly do if we did that. So hopefully that's still ahead for us at the right time."
Whether the Freeman Gambit pays off over the next two weeks before the upcoming postseason tournament is an open question. Gambits are risky, even when they work.

item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers will be in every game they play in October, and that alone means they will enter the playoffs as the favorites to win the World Series.
Not because of Shohei Ohtani. Not because of Freddie Freeman. And certainly not because of their bullpen.
There were a number of alarming developments in the last week or so, but if any team is designed to survive them, it’s the Dodgers.
Whatever their problems, they still have the best rotation in baseball.
No player influences the outcome of a game as much as a starting pitcher, and the Dodgers are the only team that will be able to roll out one Cy Young Award-caliber arm after another after another.
The Dodgers were negligent with Ohtani, and the verdict on their management of Freeman is pending, but they at least set up their pitchers the right way.
The rotation is more than a collection of big names. In Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell, the Dodgers have three starters who are peaking in time to deliver the kinds of performances that will be required for them to win their third consecutive World Series.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto pitched seven shutout innings on Tuesday in a 4-0 win over the Cincinnati Reds, marking his third consecutive seven-inning start.
“I feel really good and I don’t have any physical problems,” Yamamoto told reporters in Japanese. “I want to treat practice each and every day with importance and go into October in the best condition.”
Yamamoto isn’t alone.
The day before Yamamoto’s start, Tarik Skubal pitched seven scoreless innings of his own in a 4-1 victory over the Reds. In his previous start, which was also against the Reds but at Dodger Stadium, Skubal pitched 7 ⅓ innings.
“Just getting in a rhythm,” Skubal said.
Blake Snell, who is scheduled to take his turn in the rotation on Wednesday, was 4-0 with a 1.04 earned-run average in the six games he started since returning from an elbow cleanup that cost him three months.
The one source of concern in the rotation is Tyler Glasnow, who, like Snell, was slow-played in his return from an injury. Sidelined for 3 ½ months because of back problems, Glasnow showed promise in his first couple of starts after he came back. But in his last two starts, he gave up a combined eight runs, 11 hits and seven walks in 10 innings. But as the team’s No. 4 starter, he is unlikely to start more than one game in any postseason series.
Even before Ohtani was placed on the injured list because of right arm and left knee injuries, the starting pitching was likely going to have to carry the Dodgers – much as it did last year.
Recent developments have shifted even more of the burden to the starting pitchers.
Edwin Diaz, their $69-million closer, was blow-torched for five runs in ⅔ of an inning in the most recent game of his minor-league rehabilitation assignment. At this point, he’s a longshot to make the postseason roster.
Diaz’s failure to rediscover his All-Star form will have major ramifications on the bullpen, which lost ninth-inning candidate Edgardo Henriquez to a lower-back problem for the remainder of the regular season. Henriquez’s status for the playoffs remains a mystery.
Manager Dave Roberts’ current ninth-inning choice, Tanner Scott, is in a minor slump, as he has given up runs in five of his last 12 apperances.
While the Dodgers will have to find a closer – Roki Sasaki? – their ability to create favorable matchups in the innings before the ninth is also under question. The simplest way to address those uncertainties will be for the starters to pitch deeper into games. Last year, Yamamoto pitched a complete game in the National League Championship Series and another in his next start in the World Series. Snell had an eight-inning start in the NLCS.
The greater problem could be the already-inconsistent offense, which could go into the playoffs with physically-compromised versions of Ohtani and Freeman.
Freeman missed three of five games before starting at first base on Tuesday. Freeman collected three hits in the game, but he’s 37 years old and the Dodgers can’t be certain how his right knee will hold up.
As for Ohtani, Roberts reported on Tuesday that he resumed baseball activities. Roberts said he expected Ohtani to return before the end of the regular season, but hedged his prediction.
“Whether it happens or not,” Roberts said, “is to be determined.”
If the Dodgers don’t know if Ohtani will be able to even step into the batter’s box next week, how could they possibly count on him to be a consistent source of offense?
They can’t.
In other words, the margin for error could be miniscule for the Dodgers. Their starting pitchers might have to be close to perfect. The challenge will be formidable. But considering who will be pitching for them, it will be very much in the realm of possibility.

The Los Angeles Dodgers clinched a postseason spot for the 14th consecutive season and are closing in on a 13th National League West title during that span.
Also of importance for the Dodgers is finishing with a top two record in the NL as it would come with a first-round bye in the playoffs. That could be of particular value to a slew of injured Dodgers, including Shohei Ohtani, Andy Pages, Dalton Rushing and Edgardo Henriquez.
Dodgers updates
Dalton Rushing
Rushing made a surprising return on Sept. 1 from a slight tear in the UCL of his right elbow, but only managed to appear in four games off the bench before going back on the 10-day injured list. That came after Rushing was scratched from the lineup due to right elbow trouble that stemmed from his attempt at a throwing progression.
The Dodgers have since ruled out Rushing possibly catching again this year, but they remain hopeful he will be an option as a left-handed bat off the bench.
“Dalton’s doing well,” manager Dave Roberts said on SportsNet LA. “Building up his progression.”
Shohei Ohtani
Ohtani started his swinging progression on Tuesday by hitting off a tee. Roberts said he “felt good” doing so and is going to continue moving along.
“I don’t know what’s in store for tomorrow, but I know there’s going to be a consistent buildup. Don’t know when the time to return to play is, but today was positive and hopefully we can just keep building toward that,” Roberts said.
Roberts added he believes Ohtani will return at some point in the regular season, but cautioned, “Whether it happens or not is to be determined.”
Ohtani is eligible to be activated off the 15-day injured list Sept. 23.
Andy Pages
Pages has been swinging a bat for several days and took a step forward on Tuesday by hitting off pitching machine. Next for Pages is to log at-bats against the Trajekt machine.
Edgardo Henriquez
Henriquez, the latest Dodgers injury, returned to Los Angeles in order to undergo testing on his back/side area. He was officially put on the 15-day injured list due to low back discomfort, but Roberts noted there might be some trouble with the oblique as well.
Henriquez is not eligible to return during the regular season but the Dodgers hope he will be available for the playoffs.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are in familiar territory with the playoffs less than two weeks away. They are once again looking for answers in their bullpen. The Dodgers have placed Edgardo Henriquez on the IL with lower back discomfort, and he has been ruled out for the remainder of the regular season.
Henriquez has been placed on the 15-day IL, but there remains a path for him returning during the playoffs if all goes well. While the Dodgers made Edwin Diaz a priority this past offseason, it has been Henriquez who has kept the bullpen together.
Through 61 appearances, Henriquez had a 2.85 ERA while striking out over 29% of the hitters he's faced. If he's unable to return to LA's bullpen during the playoffs, the unit is suddenly facing a problem.
Edgardo Henriquez injury leaves Dodgers facing reality they desperately wanted to avoid
While the Dodgers have a healthy amount of left-handed options in the bullpen — considering Tanner Scott once again becoming an effective option at the end of games — as well as Alex Vesia and Jack Dreyer, they don't really have an established option among righties.
Brock Stewart hasn't looked bad this season, but injuries have limited him to just 22 innings pitched this season. Evan Phillips is back in the bullpen, and while he has 3.68 ERA through 27 appearances, his FIP of 4.65 makes him a regression candidate ahead of the playoffs.
It also doesn't help matters that the Dodgers aren't viewing the return of Diaz as a potential solution. He is currently on a minor-league rehab assignment, but the results simply haven't been there. It's forced Dave Roberts to offer a blunt assessment on Diaz earlier this week, suggesting there's a chance he's left off the playoff roster if he can't overcome his current struggles.
That is why Henriquez's injury is such a blow. He was a clear answer for what the Dodgers lacked in the bullpen, and coupling that with Diaz's struggles, Roberts and Co. are back at the drawing board. Perhaps Kris Bubic could be an answer. Bubic is with the Dodgers after a successful rehab assignment earlier this month and is expected to be reinstated from the IL in the coming days.
If there is a silver lining for the Dodgers, outside of Shohei Ohtani, their starting rotation is healthy and that could ultimately prove to be the difference-maker during the playoffs.

The Los Angeles Dodgers made Edwin Diaz the highest paid closer over the offseason. Now, he might not even make the postseason roster.
Diaz had a rehab outing Sunday in which he faced eight batters, retiring only two while walking three and hitting a batter. He threw 30 pitches to get those two outs, with only 13 strikes. Manager Dave Roberts talked about his recent woes on Monday before the Dodgers game against the Cincinnati Reds.
“He needs to pitch better. It hasn’t been good,” Roberts said on Monday. “He’s going to pitch on Wednesday, and I guess we’ll evaluate then. I think the world of him. The baseball card looks great. But where we’re at, there’s got to be something for us to be able to hang our hat on. And he knows that. He knows that. He wants to pitch well. So for me, Wednesday, we’ll be watching closely.”
He also acknowledged that Diaz might not make the postseason roster.
“Yeah … we have to go with our best pitchers, as far as performance, talent, all that stuff. So my bet is that he will be (one of them). But again, there’s got to be some kind of evidence or something for us, again, to sort of bet on. My bet is yes, but we still have to see something.”
Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic has more on the terrible season overall that Diaz has had as a Dodger here.
The Dodgers are already down another reliever, at least for the rest of the regular season. Edgardo Henriquez went on the IL on Monday with lower back discomfort. Bobby Miller was recalled from Triple-A Oklahoma City. Right-hander Paul Gervase and left-hander Kris Bubic also joined the team in Cincinnati. Gervase was added to the active roster, and Bubic could be added in the coming days.
Roki Sasaki has been sidelines with a blister and is tentatively scheduled to pitch on Thursday in Cincinnati. However, the weather is supposed to be hot and humid, and the team is worried about how that will affect Sasaki’s blister.
“We just can’t put him in a position to go backward. And so obviously people can look at Thursday. But again, if he can’t do it without accomplishing it, finishing a start, and not regress, then it’s not worth it. So I think for us, we’re just keeping it open-ended right now.”

CINCINNATI -- At one point this season, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts proclaimed his "trust tree" of high-leverage bullpen arms to be as large as it had been in quite some time. But in the final two weeks before the postseason, his proverbial tree has grown far more bare.
The Dodgers lost hard-throwing right-hander Edgardo Henriquez, who had emerged as one of the team's most reliable relievers, to the 15-day injured list due to lower back discomfort before Monday's postseason-clinching 4-1 win over the Reds.
Henriquez is not eligible to return during the regular season, but the Dodgers are hopeful he could return for the playoffs. The team will know more after Henriquez undergoes imaging on his back and side.
The loss of Henriquez came after Roberts acknowledged that the rehabbing Edwin Díaz could be pitching himself out of a postseason bullpen role if he does not show improvement in what could be his final rehab outing with Triple-A Oklahoma City on Wednesday.
Right-handers Paul Gervase and Bobby Miller were recalled from Triple-A to shore up the bullpen on Monday.
As the most important games of the year draw near, the Dodgers' bullpen situation is starting to feel similar to last year, when they had more questions than answers for piecing together the late innings.
Henriquez posted a 2.85 ERA through 60 innings, striking out 71 against 25 walks. He hit 103 mph or higher 17 times, more than any Major League pitcher not named Jacob Misiorowski (140 pitches) or Mason Miller (33 pitches). But Henriquez became more than just a hard thrower this year, developing the command and the confidence to be a leverage weapon for the Dodgers.
With Díaz on the IL as he deals with inflammation on the right side of his neck, the Dodgers have not had a set closer, although Tanner Scott has gotten the bulk of save situations. Henriquez established himself as not only part of the bridge to the ninth inning, but also as a legitimate option to close out games.
"He’s got just really electric stuff, and in the ninth inning that stuff plays," Roberts said earlier this month. "In all honesty, there’s four or five guys that I feel can finish a game. But yeah, Edgardo is certainly high up the rungs."
The Dodgers have not seen enough from Díaz on his rehab assignment -- which was initially expected to span just a couple of outings -- to bring him back to the bullpen, further complicating the leverage picture.
Through four outings with Oklahoma City, Díaz has allowed six earned runs in 3 1/3 innings. He has struggled mightily with his command, issuing seven walks against four strikeouts. The hope was that he could use the stint in the Minors to work on his mechanical issues, but it is unclear whether he has made much progress.
Accordingly, it's questionable whether the Dodgers can afford to carry this version of Díaz on the postseason roster.
"We have to go with our best pitchers, as far as performance, talent, all that stuff," Roberts said. "My bet is that he will be [on the postseason roster]. But again, there's got to be some kind of evidence or something for us, again, to sort of bet on. So my bet is yes, but we still got to see something."
Díaz is on his second IL stint of the year after having surgery to remove loose bodies from his right elbow in April. In the first season of his three-year, $69 million contract with the Dodgers, Díaz has recorded an 11.85 ERA and blown four of his 11 save opportunities.
Roberts has already said that Díaz is set to pitch in lower leverage, rather than return to the closer role, when he's activated. If Díaz can earn back the ninth inning -- or any leverage opportunities -- it would partially solve the Dodgers' growing bullpen problem. But it comes down to whether he can perform when called on.
"He needs to pitch better. It hasn't been good," Roberts said. "He's going to pitch on Wednesday, and so I guess we'll evaluate then. I think the world of him. The baseball card looks great. But it's like, where we're at, there's got to be something for us to be able to hang our hat on. And he knows that. He wants to pitch well."

By Field Level Media
Sep 15 (Field Level Media) – The Los Angeles Dodgers put relief pitcher Edgardo Henriquez on the 15-day injured list due to lower back discomfort on Monday, ending the right-hander’s regular season and causing more upheaval for the team’s bullpen.
Los Angeles has also been nursing Edwin Diaz back in a slow recovery from right elbow surgery with recent Triple-A outings that have not proven successful.
In his most recent appearance for Oklahoma City, Diaz struggled through two- thirds of an inning on Sunday, allowing five runs and three walks in a performance that Dodgers manager Dave Roberts admitted wasn’t going to be enough to merit a promotion.
The Dodgers have left open the possibility for Henriquez to return in the postseason.
Henriquez, 24, has appeared in 61 games (one start) this season, posting a 2.85 ERA with 71 strikeouts against 25 walks in 60 innings.
Diaz, a three-time All-Star, has struggled this season in limited action, logging seven saves in 11 opportunities and an 11.85 ERA in 16 appearances.
Los Angeles recalled right-handed pitchers Paul Gervase and Bobby Miller from Triple-A to help shore up their shaky bullpen. Emmet Sheehan was sent to Oklahoma City after throwing six shutout innings in a start against the Miami Marlins on Sunday.
Gervase, 26, has a 2.35 ERA over four major league appearances this season. He owns a lifetime 3.38 ERA with no decisions in 10 outings, all in relief, for the Tampa Bay Rays (2025) and Los Angeles (2025-26).
Miller, 27, has made one big-league appearance in 2026, earning a win over the Washington Nationals on Sept. 6 with three innings of one-run relief. He is 14-8 with a 5.40 ERA in 38 outings (36 starts) for the Dodgers over parts of four seasons.
Sheehan, 26, is 5-8 with a 4.79 ERA in 22 starts this year, 15-12 with a 4.23 ERA in 50 career appearances (45 starts), all with Los Angeles.
(–Field Level Media)

Dodgers might be forced to leave Edwin Díaz off postseason roster
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” from the closer to put him on the playoff roster.
- The Dodgers placed reliever Edgardo Henriquez on the 15-day injured list and recalled Bobby Miller and Paul Gervase.
CINCINNATI — Even as the Dodgers clinched a postseason berth with their 4-1 win over the Reds on Monday, bullpen uncertainty loomed.
When they get to the playoffs, who’s going to take the ball in high-leverage situations?
Their options are dwindling. Edgardo Henriquez landed on the 15-day injured list Monday with low back discomfort, ruling him out for the rest of the regular season. Edwin Díaz was so shaky in his rehab assignment Sunday that a spot on the postseason roster isn’t guaranteed.
“We have to go with our best pitchers, as far as performance, talent, all that stuff,” manager Dave Roberts said before the Dodgers opened a four-game series against the Reds. “So my bet is that he will be [on the roster]. But there’s got to be some kind of evidence or something for us to sort of bet on. And so my bet is, yes, but we’ve still got to see something.”
The Dodgers clinch a playoff berth with their 4-1 victory over the Cincinnati Reds, reaching the postseason for a record-tying 14th consecutive year.
Díaz (neck) had the worst outing of his triple-A rehab assignment, surrendering five runs and issuing two walks in two-thirds of an inning. The dud put his return timeline in doubt. His next rehab appearance is scheduled for Wednesday.
“I think the world of him, the baseball card looks great,” Roberts said. “But where we’re at, there’s got to be something for us to be able to hang our hat on. And he knows that. He knows that. He wants to pitch well. So for me, Wednesday, we’ll be watching closely.”
So, who’s still in play?
Tanner Scott remains Roberts’ go-to in save situations. And Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Jack Dreyer and Blake Treinen all have experience in late innings.
On Monday, starter Tarik Skubal gave the group a much-needed break with seven shutout innings. He limited the Reds to three hits and a walk, cruising through their lineup almost three times in 90 pitches.
The Dodgers pulled ahead by four runs, on home runs from Kyle Tucker and Teoscar Hernández, who have both broken out of slumps, and an RBI single from Kiké Hernández.
With the game still relatively tight, Vesia entered in the bottom of the eighth to face the left-handed heavy bottom of the order. He retired the side.
Phillips and Treinen both were warming in the ninth when the Dodgers got a runner to second base with one out. When they failed to score him, Phillips jogged in to face the top of the order. He surrendered a high-flying solo homer to Elly De La Cruz on a fastball above the zone but avoided further damage.
Before the game, the Dodgers added two fresh arms to the bullpen. They recalled right-handers Bobby Miller and Paul Gervase, as they put Henriquez on the IL and optioned right-hander Emmet Sheehan.
Henriquez will undergo imaging on the area, which Roberts said stretched to his side near his oblique.
“The hope is we’ll get him back in the postseason,” Roberts said.
Roberts said he didn’t know what the move meant for Sheehan, who in his past two starts limited opponents to one run and recorded 15 strikeouts in a combined 11 ⅔ innings.
“Some of it’s probably contingent on Roki [Sasaki], and we’ve got another start coming up down the road here, as far as a bullpen kind of situation,” Roberts said. “So I don’t know, but Emmet’s done everything he can do in his power to force our hand, which I love. The last two have been really good.”
Sasaki (right middle finger blister) could start Thursday. His bullpen session Monday marked the first time he had tested covering the sensitive area on his finger with Dermabond, Roberts said.
“We just can’t put him in a position to go backward,” Roberts said.
The Dodgers also have more bullpen reinforcements coming.
Another bullpen addition is left-hander Kris Bubic, who met the team in Cincinnati and is in place to make his Dodgers debut later this week. Bubic made his last rehab appearance for triple-A Oklahoma City on Sunday, so Roberts said the Dodgers likely won’t activate him off the 60-day injured list until Wednesday at the earliest.
The Dodgers acquired Bubic from the Kansas City Royals at the trade deadline this year. He’d been on the IL since May, first with a low-grade flexor strain in his left forearm, and then a shoulder impingement setback.
In six triple-A rehab appearances over 5⅔ innings, Bubic didn’t yield a run and he limited opponents to two hits and two walks.
Roberts was noncommittal about Bubic being a high-leverage option.
“Seems like all of our games are leverage these days,” he said.
By not putting Shohei Ohtani on the injured list in July or in August, the Dodgers may have compromised the two-way star’s ability to be healthy for the playoffs.

The Los Angeles Dodgers placed right-hander Edgardo Henriquez on the 15-day injured list Monday with low back discomfort, ending his 2026 regular season. Los Angeles recalled Bobby Miller from Triple-A Oklahoma City as the corresponding roster move.
Henriquez had developed into a regular bullpen option during his first full major league season, making 61 appearances. MLB.com's Sonja Chen took to X, formerly Twitter, shortly after the club announced the transaction and noted the calendar implications of Henriquez's IL placement.
"Henriquez going on the 15-day IL ends his regular season."

Henriquez last pitched Sunday vs. the Miami Marlins, allowing two earned runs on three hits and one walk over two-thirds of an inning. He also recorded one strikeout and received credit for a hold in Los Angeles' 6-4 loss.
The 24-year-old right-hander finishes the regular season with a 4-1 record and 2.85 ERA across 61 games, including one start. The right-hander struck out 71 and walked 25 over 60 innings while posting a 1.03 WHIP. His 61 appearances ranked 24th in the National League.

The move does not automatically rule him out for the postseason if he recovers and earns a roster spot.

CINCINNATI — The Los Angeles Dodgers set out this winter to address the closer position for good. Instead, they’re facing the possibility that a reliever they signed as a star free agent will be excluded from their postseason plans for a second consecutive season.
Edwin Díaz continues to struggle, as Tanner Scott did a year ago, and his rehab assignment with Triple-A Oklahoma City has gone poorly enough that Dodgers manager Dave Roberts acknowledged Monday the club could leave the three-time All-Star closer off the postseason roster. Against minor-leaguers Sunday, Díaz surrendered five runs, walked three, hit a batter and recorded just two outs in his worst appearance yet.
Advertisement
“We have to go with our best pitchers, as far as performance, talent, all that stuff,” Roberts said. “So my bet is that he will be (on the roster). But again, there’s got to be some kind of evidence or something for us, again, to sort of bet on. And so my bet is yes, but we still got to see something.”
The Dodgers gave Díaz three years and $69 million to address a bullpen that floundered in 2025. They won their second consecutive World Series despite Scott — who signed a four-year, $72 million contract — not appearing in a single playoff game.
A second plunge into the deep end of the relief market brought even worse results than the 4.74 ERA and league-worst 10 blown saves Scott had in 2025. Díaz’s famous trumpets have sounded more like a sad trombone.
Díaz’s 16 appearances with the Dodgers yielded a disastrous 11.85 ERA. He missed three months due to arthroscopic surgery to remove loose bodies in his right elbow. Upon his return, he struggled enough that the Dodgers almost immediately put him back on the injured list for what they called a neck issue. They believed his struggles were mechanical, citing the lowest arm angle of his career (14.9 degrees) as a reason his stuff and command were nowhere near where they needed to be.
Attempts to correct the issue have not worked. What was supposed to be a pair of rehab outings has been extended. The organization thought Sunday’s outing could be the final step before activation, with Díaz joining the team in Cincinnati this week to try to re-earn his closer’s job.
But Díaz has allowed six runs and walked seven of the 21 batters he’s faced since starting his rehab. Even more concerning is how Díaz’s delivery seems even more out of whack than before. His fastball still lacks the north-south movement that it needs to succeed. On that pitch this season, he’s averaged 11.8 inches of induced vertical break, which measures how much “hop” or “ride” the pitch generates. The 15 fastballs he threw Sunday generated just 9.7 inches of IVB.
There’s plenty for Díaz to fix, and not a lot of time.
Advertisement
“He needs to pitch better,” Roberts said. “I think the world of him. The baseball card looks great. But it’s like, where we’re at, there’s got to be something for us to be able to hang our hat on. And he knows that. He knows that. He wants to pitch well.”
So the Dodgers summoned rehabbing reliever Kris Bubic to join the big club Monday instead. Bubic is expected to pitch as soon as Wednesday, Roberts said. Bubic, a former All-Star starting pitcher with the Kansas City Royals, was acquired at the trade deadline and has thrown 5 2/3 scoreless innings with nine strikeouts on his rehab assignment since the trade.
Díaz will stick with Oklahoma City for at least one more outing on Wednesday, and the organization will evaluate from there, Roberts said.
The Dodgers will spend the coming days trying to sort out how they will attack the ninth inning. One option went on the IL on Monday, when the Dodgers placed hard-throwing reliever Edgardo Henriquez on the shelf with a lower back issue; Henriquez has been the Dodgers’ most effective reliever recently, with a 1.69 ERA since Aug. 5. Now, his regular season is over.
Scott, who has bounced back this year with a 2.91 ERA, will be part of fixing the ninth-inning problem they thought they’d avoid entirely when they signed Díaz.

One day after allowing his first runs in four weeks, Dodgers reliever Edgardo Henríquez was placed on the 15-day injured list with lower back discomfort. His regular season is over.
Henríquez has been one of the best relievers on the team this season, with a 2.85 ERA and 2.47 xERA in 61 games, with 71 strikeouts and 25 walks in 60 innings, with a 29.3-percent strikeout rate and only one home run allowed. The 24-year-old leads the Dodgers bullpen in innings and xERA, and is second only to Tanner Scott in strikeouts.
Sunday was a rare rough outing for Henríquez, who allowed three hits, a walk, and two runs in the eighth inning, recording only two outs. Those were the first runs allowed by Henríquez since August 16, snapping a string of 11 consecutive scoreless appearances.
“It’s the confidence he has in his fastball. Everybody knows it’s not easy to hit 103, 104 coming at you with confidence,” outfielder Teoscar Hernández said last week on the Dodgers’ homestand. “That’s been the difference between the Edgardo we saw at the beginning of the year, and the Edgardo we’re seeing right now.”
Whether Henriquez will be ready and available once the postseason starts remains to be seen.
With Henríquez sidelined, Bobby Miller was recalled from Triple-A Oklahoma City. Miller was just optioned last Monday, but he’s able to return before his 15 days are up because he’s replacing an injured player.
Miller pitched once for Oklahoma City after getting optioned, and it was a rough outing, with five runs allowed in 1 2/3 innings on Friday against Sugar Land, with all five runs scored on two home runs by the same player.

MIAMI –– The Dodgers’ bullpen melted down once again on Sunday in Miami.
Only this time, they got an unhelpful hand from some shaky late-game defense.
In a 6-4 loss to the Miami Marlins, the Dodgers allowed all of the scoring in the final two innings of what became a walk-off defeat; watching three high-leverage relievers –– Edgardo Henriquez, Tanner Scott and Brock Stewart –– falter after their infield gave away extra outs behind them.
In Henriquez’s two-run eighth inning, one would-be groundout instead snuck between shortstop Mookie Betts and second baseman Miguel Rojas, leaving Rojas injured after he made a late sliding attempt. Another got stuck in Betts’ hand while he tried to make a charging throw on the run, gifting the Marlins a free scoring opportunity that would lead to a two-run single from Otto Lopez.
The four-run ninth inning, which was capped off by Agustín Ramírez’s walk-off homer against Stewart, was just as frustrating, as Scott’s bid for a four-out save imploded after a pair of infield singles; one on a bunt, and another on a bad underhand flipped from a hobbled Freddie Freeman at first base.
“When you give a team extra outs,” manager Dave Roberts said, “that’s what happens.”
Initially, it appeared as though the Dodgers might still escape.
After Lopez’s single in the eighth, Scott replaced Henriquez to face Griffin Conine and struck him out on three pitches to end the inning and keep a 3-2 lead intact.
In the top of the ninth, the Dodgers added to the advantage on Betts’ RBI double, giving them “enough to win” offensively, as Roberts put it, even though they left the bases loaded later in the frame.
Alas, the bottom of the ninth immediately went sideways on an Xavier Edwards ground ball to lead off the inning.
Freeman, who has been playing through a knee injury and is mired in a 1-for-26 slump, fielded the ball but made a bad underhand flip back to first. Scott had to adjust to it as he went to cover the base, and was too late to recover as Edwards beat the play out.
Jakob Marsee came up next and executed a perfect bunt inside the third-base line.
Then, Javier Sanoja got jammed by a slider but still muscled a two-run double into the left-field corner.
Just like that, the Dodgers’ lead was gone. It was only Scott’s fourth blown save in 26 opportunities this season, but also the sixth time in his last 11 outings he has given up a run.
“Actually, I think the last week has been really good as far as the stuff,” Roberts said when asked of that trend, which has pushed Scott’s ERA to 2.91. “Today I think was just an odd day.”
Four pitches later, the game was over. Stewart came in to face the pinch-hitting Ramírez, but grooved him a fastball that was launched to left for the walk-off blast.
“It was supposed to be up above the zone. That’s where my fastball plays best,” Stewart said. “Just missed my spot, threw it right down the middle.”
Thus, the Dodgers suffered a loss that wasted big days from Emmet Sheehan (who threw six scoreless innings in his start) and Josue De Paula (who mashed a monstrous three-run home run in the fourth inning for his first career hit), while also delaying any possibility of clinching a playoff spot for a second-straight day.
“It’s baseball,” Roberts said. “It sucks. It feels bad. But that’s part of the thing.”
With a sigh, he later added: “But yeah, today was a crappy one.”
